unit: cents less earned per dollar of prize (marginal propensity to consume leisure, about 11%)
period: Massachusetts lottery players surveyed in the mid-1980s
note: 'unearned income reduces labor earnings, with a marginal propensity to consume leisure of approximately 11 percent, with larger effects for individuals between 55 and 65 years old'; prizes paid yearly over 20 years (Imbens, Rubin and Sacerdote, AER 91(4), 2001, abstract)
sample of the survey; earlier NBER working paper 7001 (1999) gives 496 observations

unit: age from which the effect is larger (55 to 65)
note: larger effects for winners aged 55 to 65 (abstract)

unit: % of the prize, fall in pre-tax earnings per year
period: Swedish lottery winners, over more than ten years
note: 'Pretax earnings fall by approximately 1.1 percent of the prize amount per year. A windfall gain of 1 million SEK (about US$140,000) thus reduces annual earnings by about 11,000 SEK, corresponding to 5.5 percent of the sample average' (Cesarini, Lindqvist, Notowidigdo and Östling, AER 107(12), 2017, introduction); the reduction is 'immediate, persistent, and quite similar by age, education, and sex' (abstract)

unit: percentage points lower labour force participation per 1 million SEK won
period: up to five years after the win

note: pooled sample of three Swedish lotteries; prizes total 4,662 million SEK, about US$650 million (Cesarini et al. 2017, section II)

unit: lifetime marginal propensity to earn out of unearned income (negative), at age 20 and age 60
note: 'lifetime marginal propensities to earn out of unearned income from -0.17 at age 20 to -0.04 at age 60' (abstract)

unit: cents less household labour earnings per extra dollar of unearned income
note: 'an extra $1 of unearned income in a given period reduces household labor earnings by about 50 cents, decreases total labor taxes by 10 cents, and increases consumption expenditure by 60 cents'; 'households in higher quartiles of the income distribution reducing their earnings by a larger amount' (Golosov, Graber, Mogstad and Novgorodsky, QJE 139(2), 2024, abstract)

unit: USD less annual earnings per USD 100 won, in each of the five years after the win
note: 'for an extra 100 dollars in wealth, winners reduce their earnings on average by 2.3 dollars in each of the five subsequent years'; households in the bottom quartile of pre-win income reduce annual household labor earnings by 1.3 dollars per 100 dollars, the top quartile by 3.1 dollars; 'the probability that the winner is employed decreases by 3.7 percentage points per 100,000 dollars' (working paper version of January 2023, not the published text)

unit: times: the fall in the probability of employment for the lowest income quartile relative to the highest (more than)
note: 'The lower-income households, however, are more likely to stop working – the reduction in the probability of employment for the winners in the lowest quartile is more than twice as large as that of the winners in the highest quartile' (January 2023 working paper)

unit: US lottery winners of working age (21 to 64) with wins of at least $30,000
note: Table 2.1 of the January 2023 working paper (also NBER working paper 29000, July 2021): winners aged 21 to 64 with wins of at least $30,000, from US tax records

unit: EUR lower earnings after one year per EUR 100,000 won (about EUR 1,800 after three years)
note: 'a lottery prize of €100,000 leads to a drop in earnings of about €1,100 after 1 year, of €1,600 after two years, and of almost €1,800 after 3 years' (IZA DP 9472, 2015); published version: 'The effects are small but statistically significant. We do not find a significant effect of lottery prizes on the probability of being employed' (Picchio, Suetens and van Ours, Economic Journal 128(611), 2018, abstract)

unit: % of US workers who would stop working if they won $10 million (about two thirds would keep working)
note: telephone survey of 1,039 adults employed full or part time, margin of error ±3 points; in earlier Gallup surveys 39% to 44% said they would quit (Gallup, 14 August 2013)

unit: % who would keep working if they had enough money to live on without other income
note: internet survey of 1,361 working members of a prize-site panel (ChangeField, ここワンリサーチ, released 28 September 2015), not a random sample: keep the current job 49.8%, change jobs 16.0%, start a business 9.7%
